# Octree-based Volume Rendering

Also called: Chamberlain's algorithm, LaMar's algorithm, Weiler's smoothing

## Overview
Octree-based volume rendering accelerates image-order ray casting by recursively traversing a hierarchical spatial subdivision of volumetric data, using projected size and field-of-view criteria to select nodes for approximation or culling [S1]. It differs from sibling methods like [Point Plane Test Traversal](982-point-plane-test-traversal.md) by using a tree structure for adaptive level-of-detail selection rather than fixed coarse meshes or plane tests, and unlike [CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal](2455-cpu-sparse-voxel-octree-traversal.md) which focuses on explicit sparse storage, this method traditionally assumes the octree resides in main memory [S1].

## How it works
**Inputs:** Volumetric dataset (density $\sigma$ and color $c$); camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, field-of-view) [G].
**Outputs:** Rendered image [G].

**Data Structures:**
*   **Octree Node:** Contains a bounding box, a pointer to children (if not a leaf), and leaf data [G].
*   **Leaf Data:** For traditional methods, scalar density and color values [S1]. For PlenOctree, density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients [S2].

**Steps:**
1.  **Preprocessing:** Perform octree subdivision of the volumetric data [S1].
2.  **Rendering:** Recursively traverse the octree [S1].
3.  **Selection:** Compute the projected size of each octree node on the fly [S1]. If the size is smaller than a predefined threshold, consider the node sufficiently accurate to approximate all nodes below it [S1].
4.  **LaMar’s Criteria:** Use two filters: distance (similar to Chamberlain) and field-of-view [S1]. Discard nodes that do not intersect the view frustum [S1]. Select nodes whose projected angle is less than half the field-of-view angle [S1].
5.  **Smoothing (Weiler):** Apply an extension to smooth the discontinuity artifacts at LOD boundaries [S1].

**PlenOctree Variant Steps:**
1.  **Intersection:** For each ray, determine ray-voxel intersections in the octree structure, producing a sequence of segments between voxel boundaries with constant density and color, of lengths $\{\delta_i\}$ [S2].
2.  **Accumulation:** Apply NeRF’s volume rendering model:
    $$ C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=0}^{N} T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)) \mathbf{c}_i $$
    where transmittance $T_i = \exp(-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j)$ [S2].
3.  **Early Stopping:** Stop rendering when accumulated transmittance $T_i < \gamma$, where $\gamma = 0.01$ [S2].

**Parameters:** Predefined threshold for projected size [S1]; early-stopping transmittance threshold $\gamma = 0.01$ [S2].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
*   **LOD Artifacts:** Substantial visual artifacts appear at the boundaries of different levels of detail due to inconsistencies of the view-plane at different levels of detail [S1].
*   **Memory Limitation:** Inability to reduce the volumetric data size in main memory, limiting the ability to render datasets larger than main memory size [S1].

## Subtopics

### PlenOctree Rendering
A variant that converts a trained NeRF-SH model into a sparse octree representation for real-time rendering [S2]. It sets itself apart from traditional octree methods by storing density and SH coefficients to model view-dependent appearance, rather than scalar values [S2]. Choose it when real-time rendering of [neural radiance fields](#906-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) is required [S2]. See [Hierarchical Traversal](896-hierarchical-traversal.md).

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** Depends on octree depth and data sparsity [G]. LaMar’s algorithm provides a considerable speedup over Chamberlain’s algorithm by using FOV culling [S1].
*   **Memory Complexity:** Traditional methods require the entire octree in main memory, limiting scalability to datasets larger than RAM [S1]. PlenOctree uses sparse storage, reducing memory footprint [S2].
*   **Measured Performance:** PlenOctree achieves ~42 FPS on Tanks and Temples scenes at 1920×1080 resolution, maintaining comparable image quality metrics (PSNR/SSIM) to [standard NeRF](#910-nerf-mlp-architecture.md) [S2].
*   **Strengths:** FOV culling improves performance [S1].
*   **Limitations:** LOD boundary artifacts require smoothing; memory-bound for large datasets in traditional implementations [S1].
*   **When to Use:** Real-time rendering of volumetric data with significant empty space or uniform regions; when memory allows loading the octree [G].
*   **When Not to Use:** Datasets exceeding main memory size without sparse storage extensions; scenes requiring seamless LOD transitions without post-processing smoothing [S1].

## Background
The octree spatial hierarchy was first proposed by Chamberlain et al. for rendering surface (polygonal) geometry [S1]. LaMar et al. improved selection criteria with distance and FOV filters [S1]. Weiler et al. addressed LOD artifacts with smoothing extensions [S1]. PlenOctree extends this to neural radiance fields, enabling real-time rendering of NeRFs [S2].

## Sources
[S1] A system for real-time rendering of compressed time-varying volume data, https://doi.org/10.7939/r3041m, fetched 2026-10-26
[S2] PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), http://alexyu.net/plenoctrees/, fetched 2026-10-28
